policy_title: Modernise Employment Rights for the Gig Economy
stated: Modernise employment rights to make them fit for the age of the ‘gig economy’ by establishing a new ‘dependent contractor’ employment status in between employment and self-employment (with entitlements to basic rights such as minimum earnings levels, sick pay and holiday entitlement), reviewing the tax and National Insurance status of employees, dependent contractors and freelancers to ensure fair and comparable treatment, setting a 20% higher minimum wage for people on zero-hour contracts at times of normal demand, giving a right to request a fixed-hours contract after 12 months for ‘zero hours’ and agency workers (not to be unreasonably refused), reviewing rules concerning pensions for gig economy workers, and shifting the burden of proof in employment tribunals regarding employment status from individual to employer.

source.quote: Modernise employment rights to make them fit for the age of the ‘gig economy’, including by: Establishing a new ‘dependent contractor’ employment status in between employment and self-employment, with entitlements to basic rights such as minimum earnings levels, sick pay and holiday entitlement. Reviewing the tax and National Insurance status of employees, dependent contractors and freelancers to ensure fair and comparable treatment. Setting a 20% higher minimum wage for people on zero-hour contracts at times of normal demand to compensate them for the uncertainty of fluctuating hours of work. Giving a right to request a fixed-hours contract after 12 months for ‘zero hours’ and agency workers, not to be unreasonably refused. Reviewing rules concerning pensions so that those in the gig economy don’t lose out, and portability between roles is protected. Shifting the burden of proof in employment tribunals regarding employment status from individual to employer.

bearing_set.reason: Directly targets pay levels, job security, employment rights and conditions for gig/zero-hours workers, including minimum earnings, sick pay, holiday entitlement and burden-of-proof shift in tribunals.

Explicitly includes a review of pension rules for gig economy workers, a group largely excluded from auto-enrolment, making a non-negligible verdict on pensioner poverty and private pension adequacy likely.

Mandating a 20% wage premium on zero-hours contracts and imposing new employer obligations (sick pay, holiday, pension, tribunal liability) materially raises labour costs for gig-platform businesses, creating a plausible and contested effect on firm formation, business investment and the volume of gig-sector opportunities — specific O13 indicators the evidence disputes (labour-cost vs productivity/spending-power channels).

By explicitly targeting the most precarious and lowest-paid part of the workforce (zero-hours and agency workers, gig contractors), the package is distributionally progressive — raising the income floor and compressing the gap between gig workers and more securely employed workers, moving the Gini/income-gap indicator in a narrowing direction.

membership_note: Three fundamentals: O4 is the policy's core target; O13 captures the contested labour-cost/business-dynamism tradeoff (the main cross-outcome harm mechanism); O14 captures the unambiguously redistributive direction of the package toward the lowest-paid. Tax/NI review is framed as a review only, so its direction is indeterminate and does not earn a real O11 verdict.
